payloads.expected_behavior:
Substitute the metadata service endpoint and a provider-specific path for
the target platform. Behaviour differs by provider and by configuration.

Some providers serve metadata on a link-local address over plain HTTP with
no additional request requirements. Some require a session token obtained
via a separate request before the metadata can be read. Some require a
custom request header on every metadata request. Some restrict which paths
are readable without additional configuration.

A response containing metadata content indicates the fetch reached the
service and the request was accepted. A response indicating a token or
header requirement indicates the service is present but the payload alone
is insufficient. A connection refusal or timeout does not establish that
the service is absent; it may be firewalled, hosted on a non-default
address, or unavailable from the fetch client's network position.
payloads.name: Cloud instance metadata service probe

payloads.expected_behavior: If the HTTP client or URL handler supports the file scheme, the response contains local file contents. Support depends entirely on the client library; most modern HTTP clients reject the scheme by default.
payloads.name: file scheme local read

payloads.expected_behavior: Substitute the address and port of the line-oriented service under test. Where the client supports the gopher scheme, the request delivers the decoded bytes to the target port, permitting interaction with protocols that accept commands without framing. The response is returned only if the client surfaces gopher replies.
payloads.name: gopher scheme single-command interaction

payloads.expected_behavior: Substitute a loopback address. A response body from that interface, or an error distinguishable from an unreachable-host error, indicates the fetch reached a local service. Absence of a body does not rule out execution; the response may be discarded.
payloads.name: Loopback HTTP service probe

payloads.expected_behavior: Substitute an address in a private range. A response from that address indicates the server can reach an internal network segment. Vary the substituted address across private ranges and compare responses to distinguish reachable from unreachable destinations.
payloads.name: Private range HTTP probe

payloads.expected_behavior: An authoritative nameserver under tester control records a resolution for the unique identifier. This confirms name resolution occurred. It does not by itself prove a connection was established, a request was sent, or a response was accepted. Where an HTTP callback is also available, prefer it.
payloads.name: DNS-only out-of-band callback

payloads.expected_behavior: The listener receives an HTTP request from the target server. The request method, path, headers, and source address confirm the fetch executed and identify the network position it originated from. Use a distinct identifier per injection point.
payloads.name: HTTP out-of-band callback

payloads.expected_behavior: Substitute the address and port under test. Response times differ between a port that accepts a connection and one that refuses immediately. Repeated measurements per port are required; single samples produce false positives from network noise. This is a semi-blind variant — the application does not return the destination's response, but timing leaks whether the connection was accepted.
payloads.name: Internal port reachability by timing

payloads.expected_behavior: The callback host receives an HTTP request from the target server when the webhook is triggered. The request method, path, headers, and source address reveal the origin network position and confirm the fetch was issued. Use a distinct hostname or path per test.
payloads.name: Webhook target under tester control

payloads.expected_behavior:
Substitute a hostname whose authoritative nameserver is under tester control
and configured with a low TTL and alternating answers between an allowed
address and a forbidden one.

The test succeeds if the validator resolves the allowed address and approves
the URL, and the fetch client then re-resolves the hostname within the TTL
window and reaches the forbidden address. Success is evidenced by a callback
or response from the forbidden destination.

This record documents the shape of the input; the mechanism itself is
infrastructure (authoritative nameserver, TTL, alternating records) rather
than a string. Many clients pin DNS for the duration of a request, defeating
the technique entirely. Treat a single failure as inconclusive.
payloads.name: Hostname under authoritative-DNS control

payloads.expected_behavior: This is an implementation-specific parser test, not a universally reliable host-confusion payload. URL parsers differ in how they handle backslashes in authority positions. Compare the parsed scheme, authority, hostname, and final network destination in the exact validation and fetch components. Do not assume that the backslash is normalized or treated as a path separator.
payloads.name: Backslash in authority position

payloads.expected_behavior: Substitute the target IPv4 address expressed as a single 32-bit unsigned integer in decimal. Whether the client accepts this form depends on its host parser; some clients resolve it, others reject it. Validators that require a dotted-quad string will not recognise the value as a host.
payloads.name: Decimal-encoded IPv4 host

payloads.expected_behavior: Substitute the target IPv4 address with each of its four octets expressed in hexadecimal and prefixed with 0x, joined by dots. Acceptance depends on the client's host parser. Many language HTTP clients reject hex components outright; browser and curl behaviour differs.
payloads.name: Hexadecimal-encoded IPv4 host

payloads.expected_behavior: Substitute an IPv4 address expressed in IPv4-mapped IPv6 form. An allowlist or denylist that operates on dotted-quad strings does not recognise the mapped form, while the client may resolve it to the equivalent IPv4 address. Behaviour depends on whether the client and the operating system accept mapped literals.
payloads.name: IPv6-mapped IPv4 literal

payloads.expected_behavior: Substitute the target IPv4 address with each of its four octets expressed in octal, joined by dots. Validators that parse components as decimal integers, or that require no leading zero, will not recognise the address. Whether the client accepts the form depends on its host parser.
payloads.name: Octal-encoded IPv4 host

payloads.expected_behavior: A protocol-relative reference inherits its scheme from a base URI. It is not necessarily a complete URL when supplied to a standalone HTTP client. Test only in a context that resolves references against a known base URI, and compare how the validator and fetch client resolve it.
payloads.name: Protocol-relative reference

payloads.expected_behavior: Some legacy or implementation-specific host parsers accept IPv4 addresses with fewer than four components. The interpretation is parser-dependent: the final component may represent the remaining address bits, rather than the omitted components simply being padded with zero. RFC 3986 does not establish universal acceptance of these forms. Test against the exact validator and fetch client in scope.
payloads.name: Short-form IPv4 host

payloads.expected_behavior: A validator that extracts the host by substring or by splitting before the first slash sees expected.example.com; a client that follows RFC 3986 connects to the substituted address and sends expected.example.com as userinfo. A canary listener distinguishes which component was actually used.
payloads.name: Authority ambiguity via userinfo component

payloads.expected_behavior:
The first request is sent to a permitted host under tester control. That host
responds with a 3xx status and a Location header pointing at the substituted
internal destination.

Whether this is exploitable depends on three properties of the fetch client:

- whether it follows redirects at all;
- whether it re-validates the destination of the redirect against the same
  policy applied to the original URL;
- whether it preserves properties the policy depends on (Host header,
  scheme) across the redirect.

A successful request to the internal destination — evidenced by a callback,
a response body, a timing difference, or a side effect — indicates the policy
was not re-applied after the redirect. Absence of evidence does not disprove
the vulnerability; the internal service may have been unreachable from the
fetch client's network position.
payloads.name: Redirect to unvalidated internal destination

payloads.expected_behavior: Tests a simple false comparison in a compatible string context. Compare multiple repetitions to reduce timing and content noise.
payloads.name: Boolean AND false condition

payloads.expected_behavior: Tests a simple true comparison in a compatible string context. Database comment parsing and trailing syntax vary.
payloads.name: Boolean AND true condition

payloads.expected_behavior: A false predicate for a numeric SQL expression context. Use as a paired control with the corresponding true predicate.
payloads.name: Numeric-context false predicate

payloads.expected_behavior: A true predicate for a numeric SQL expression context. The leading syntax must match the application's query structure.
payloads.name: Numeric-context true predicate

payloads.expected_behavior: A false predicate intended for a compatible quoted-string context. Response differences must be repeatable and attributable to the condition.
payloads.name: String-context false predicate

payloads.expected_behavior: A true predicate intended for a compatible quoted-string context. Compare with the paired false predicate under identical conditions.
payloads.name: String-context true predicate

payloads.expected_behavior: If evaluated in a compatible expression, SQL Server may raise a conversion error. Exact quoting and comment placement depend on the injection context.
payloads.name: SQL Server conversion error probe

payloads.expected_behavior: If evaluated in a compatible expression, PostgreSQL may raise an invalid-text-representation error. This is a DBMS-specific diagnostic probe, not a universal payload.
payloads.name: PostgreSQL invalid integer cast probe

payloads.expected_behavior: In a string-literal context, an unmatched quote may cause a SQL syntax error. Error visibility depends on application error handling.
payloads.name: Unmatched single-quote syntax probe

payloads.expected_behavior: May disrupt a parenthesized expression. The result depends on the surrounding SQL grammar and should be interpreted only alongside a baseline.
payloads.name: Unmatched parenthesis syntax probe

payloads.expected_behavior: On eligible SQL Server configurations with sufficient permissions and outbound name resolution, this may cause a DNS lookup. A callback proves name resolution only; never place query data or secrets in the hostname. High-privilege feature availability varies.
payloads.name: SQL Server DNS-only canary

payloads.expected_behavior: On eligible Oracle configurations where the account has required privileges and DNS egress is permitted, this may trigger name resolution. A callback proves resolution only; do not encode query output or secrets.
payloads.name: Oracle DNS-only canary

payloads.expected_behavior: A test string for tracing a stored value into a later query. Use only with test data; confirm the later query is parameterized or safely constructed.
payloads.name: Stored Boolean-context canary

payloads.expected_behavior: A marker for tracing stored input through later SQL construction. Comment behavior is DBMS- and context-dependent.
payloads.name: Stored comment-syntax canary

payloads.expected_behavior: A benign marker containing a quote to trace through storage and later use. It does not prove SQLi unless a later query incorporates it unsafely.
payloads.name: Stored quote canary

payloads.expected_behavior: Attempts a second, read-only constant SELECT. It is only a structural test; many application drivers reject multiple statements.
payloads.name: SQL Server harmless stacked SELECT

payloads.expected_behavior: Attempts a second, read-only constant SELECT. Support depends on connector configuration and API; do not assume multi-statements are enabled.
payloads.name: MySQL harmless stacked SELECT

payloads.expected_behavior: Attempts a second, read-only constant SELECT where the driver and query interface permit multiple statements.
payloads.name: PostgreSQL harmless stacked SELECT

payloads.expected_behavior: Requests a three-second delay where stacked statements are permitted. Driver settings and query context may reject it.
payloads.name: SQL Server short WAITFOR probe

payloads.expected_behavior: Illustrates a conditional short delay in a compatible expression context. Use low request volume and stop if service latency rises.
payloads.name: MySQL conditional delay probe

payloads.expected_behavior: Requests a short delay if the expression is evaluated. Query context, server limits, and request timeouts affect observability.
payloads.name: MySQL short delay expression

payloads.content: ' AND (SELECT CASE WHEN (1=1) THEN pg_sleep(3) ELSE pg_sleep(0) END) IS NULL--
payloads.expected_behavior: Illustrates a conditional short delay. Expression compatibility depends on query context and PostgreSQL version; validate syntax in a local lab before use.
payloads.name: PostgreSQL conditional delay probe

payloads.expected_behavior: Requests a three-second delay if stacked statements are accepted and pg_sleep is available. Driver multi-statement behavior may prevent execution. Use only in a controlled test environment.
payloads.name: PostgreSQL short delay probe

payloads.expected_behavior: A harmless marker can help identify a reflected column if the original query has two compatible columns. Replace only with a unique non-sensitive marker in a test system.
payloads.name: UNION non-sensitive canary marker (two columns)

payloads.expected_behavior: Tests whether a UNION SELECT with 1 NULL expression(s) is syntactically compatible. A successful response is not by itself proof that a particular column is reflected.
payloads.name: UNION NULL column-count probe (1)

payloads.expected_behavior: Tests whether a UNION SELECT with 2 NULL expression(s) is syntactically compatible. A successful response is not by itself proof that a particular column is reflected.
payloads.name: UNION NULL column-count probe (2)

payloads.expected_behavior: Tests whether a UNION SELECT with 3 NULL expression(s) is syntactically compatible. A successful response is not by itself proof that a particular column is reflected.
payloads.name: UNION NULL column-count probe (3)

payloads.content: ' UNION SELECT NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL--
payloads.expected_behavior: Tests whether a UNION SELECT with 4 NULL expression(s) is syntactically compatible. A successful response is not by itself proof that a particular column is reflected.
payloads.name: UNION NULL column-count probe (4)

payloads.expected_behavior: Illustrates a UNION probe in a numeric expression context. It is only applicable if the original query structure and column count are compatible.
payloads.name: UNION numeric-context column probe

techniques.description: SQL injection in which a true or false SQL condition changes an observable application response even though query results or database errors are not directly disclosed.
techniques.name: Boolean-Based Blind SQL Injection
requirements: An application feature constructs or executes SQL using input influenced by the requester.

techniques.description: SQL injection in which database or application errors reveal information about query parsing, data types, or query execution.
techniques.name: Error-Based SQL Injection
requirements: An application feature constructs or executes SQL using input influenced by the requester.

techniques.description: SQL injection in which database-side network interaction provides an out-of-band observation when the application does not return query results or useful timing differences.
techniques.name: Out-of-Band SQL Injection
requirements: An application feature constructs or executes SQL using input influenced by the requester.

techniques.description: SQL injection in which untrusted input is stored safely or apparently inert at first, then later incorporated into a dynamically constructed SQL statement in another workflow.
techniques.name: Second-Order SQL Injection
requirements: An application feature constructs or executes SQL using input influenced by the requester.

techniques.description: SQL injection in which the database driver and execution interface permit an injected statement terminator followed by an additional SQL statement.
techniques.name: Stacked-Query SQL Injection
requirements: An application feature constructs or executes SQL using input influenced by the requester.

techniques.description: Blind SQL injection in which a controlled database-side delay creates an observable timing difference that can indicate whether an injected condition was evaluated.
techniques.name: Time-Based Blind SQL Injection
requirements: An application feature constructs or executes SQL using input influenced by the requester.

techniques.description: SQL injection that uses a UNION query operator to combine attacker-controlled SELECT results with the original query result when query structure and column compatibility permit it.
techniques.name: UNION-Based SQL Injection
requirements: An application feature constructs or executes SQL using input influenced by the requester.

techniques.description: The server fetches a user-controlled destination and returns the response, allowing the requester to read the contents of internal and link-local services.
techniques.name: Basic Server-Side Request Forgery

techniques.description: The server issues a request to a user-controlled destination but does not return the response, so confirmation requires out-of-band observation, timing analysis, or side-effect detection.
techniques.name: Blind Server-Side Request Forgery

techniques.description: The hostname resolves to an allowed address at validation time and to a forbidden address at fetch time, exploiting separate resolutions rather than URL parser disagreement.
techniques.name: SSRF via DNS Rebinding

techniques.description: The validator and the fetch client interpret the URL's authority component differently, so a value that appears to target an allowed host resolves to a forbidden destination.
techniques.name: SSRF via URL Parser Confusion

techniques.description: A permitted destination returns a redirect to an unvalidated internal destination, and the fetch client follows it without re-applying the policy.
techniques.name: SSRF via Redirect Validation Failure
